claims.text: Steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications resist corrosion because they contain sufficient chromium.
Sufficient chromium causes rapid formation of a continuous chromium-rich passive layer.
The chromium-rich passive layer consists primarily of Cr2O3.
A continuous chromium-rich passive layer protects the underlying steel from corrosion.
Chromium preferentially oxidizes during exposure to corrosive conditions.
Preferential chromium oxidation produces a self-limiting passive film.
The passive film impedes transport of corrosive ions to the underlying metal.
The passive film impedes electron transport to the underlying metal.
Impeded ion and electron transport reduces the corrosion rate.
Higher-chromium steels will form thicker Cr2O3 layers than low-chromium steels under otherwise identical conditions.
Higher-chromium steels will form more uniform Cr2O3 layers than low-chromium steels under otherwise identical conditions.
Higher-chromium steels will have lower corrosion rates than low-chromium steels under otherwise identical conditions.
Low-chromium steels develop a less protective or incomplete oxide layer.
A less protective or incomplete oxide layer in low-chromium steels results in higher corrosion rates.
The proposed chromium-passivation mechanism is expected to hold at elevated temperature, defined pH, and in the presence of aggressive species such as chlorides.
The proposed mechanism may not apply under benign conditions.
The proposed mechanism may not apply under non-oxidizing conditions.
Radiation effects may modulate the corrosion resistance attributed to chromium-rich passivation.
Microstructural inhomogeneities may modulate the corrosion resistance attributed to chromium-rich passivation.
